albums.blurb: Walter Wanderley was Brazil's foremost bossa nova organist, a Recife-born bandleader with dozens of São Paulo records behind him before producer Creed Taylor brought him to New York in 1966. Rain Forest, cut at Rudy Van Gelder's studio for Verve, was his American debut, and its skipping, staccato Hammond B-3 phrasing became one of the signature sounds of the bossa craze. The album is entirely instrumental, working through Jobim and Marcos Valle tunes in a light trio setting of organ, percussion, and touches of brass and guitar.
albums.reception: The album reached No. 22 on the Billboard Top LPs chart, and its single "Summer Samba (So Nice)" hit No. 26 on the Hot 100 and No. 3 on the Easy Listening chart.

albums.blurb: The fourth album of Wonder's 1972–76 classic run, released between Innervisions and Songs in the Key of Life and recorded after the 1973 car crash that nearly killed him. It is the most inward and subdued record of that stretch — synth-heavy and largely self-played, moving between the cosmic gospel of "Heaven Is 10 Zillion Light Years Away" and the anti-Nixon funk single "You Haven't Done Nothin'," which has the Jackson 5 on backing vocals.
albums.reception: It became Wonder's first album to top the Billboard 200 and won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 1975, his second consecutive win in that category.

albums.blurb: Sampha Sisay is a South London singer and producer of Sierra Leonean descent who spent years as a behind-the-scenes collaborator — with SBTRKT, Solange, Frank Ocean, Drake, and Kanye West — before making his own full-length. Process, his 2017 debut on Young Turks, sets his cracked, keening voice against spare piano and glitching electronics, and much of it works through the death of his mother, most directly on "(No One Knows Me) Like the Piano." A second album, Lahai, followed in 2023.
albums.reception: Process won the 2017 Mercury Prize, beating shortlisted albums by Ed Sheeran, Stormzy, and The xx.
